title: Autumn Song
text:
Forgive me, dry leaf,

I cannot care for you.

I came to love in this world,

and even love I lost.

What use was weaving flowers

in the sands of the ground

if there were people sleeping

upon their own heart?


And I could not raise them up!

I weep for what I did not do

and for this weakness

that makes me sad and unhappy.

Forgive me, dry leaf!

My powerless eyes are

keeping watch and praying for those

who will not rise.


You are an autumn leaf

flying through the garden.

I leave you my nostalgia

—the best part of me.

And I go along this road,

sure of how useless everything is.

For everything is less than the wind,

less than the leaves on the ground.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the dry-leaf apostrophe and the speaker's grief over failed love, failed aid, and uselessness.

title: Song
text:
In the imbalance of the seas,

the prows turn solitary...

On one of the ships that sank

surely you were coming.


I waited for you through all the centuries

without despair and without displeasure,

and I died infinite deaths

always keeping the same face.


When the waves carried you away,

my eyes, between waters and sands,

went blind like those of statues

to everything alien to them.


My hands stopped in the air,

hardened with the wind,

lost the color they had,

and the memory of movement.


And the smile I was carrying to you

came loose and fell from me:

perhaps only it still lives

inside these endless waters.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the centuries-long waiting and the drowned ship as the place where the beloved may have been lost.

title: It Happens Thus, Anything...
text:
It happens thus—anything

serene, free, faithful.

Flower that fulfills itself, without question.

Wave that grows violent through indifferent exercise.

Moon that equally wraps the embraced lovers

and the soldiers already cold.

Also like this night air: whispering with

silences, full of births and

petals.

Equal to the halted stone, preserving its delayed destiny.

And the cloud,

light and beautiful, living from never coming to be.


The cicada burns in its music, the camel chewing

its long solitude,

The bird seeking the end of the world, the ox going

innocently toward the mountain.

It happens thus, anything serene, free, faithful.

Not like the rest of men.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the poem's catalog of faithful natural beings and the closing contrast with human restlessness.

title: From "Killing Plato" 2004:
text:
A morning in keeping with the aesthetics of a Tang-period painter:

wind

in the great acacia of the garden,

rain of yellow flowers.

She,

out of caution,

has stayed in the house and contemplates me

through

a pane of glass.

She knows that I feed on the smell of the leaves,

on the

whisper of air in the bark

of the trees,

she knows that I will return

fulfilled and scattering life everywhere.

And with how much caution she then

avoids my gaze,

with how much discretion she separates her skin from

the dark objects,

with how much softness she blurs herself

so as not to

disturb the dance of the sun in my hair.


From "Poems to My Death" 1994
editorial_note: The translation preserves Maillard's glass-separated scene, Tang-painter image, and the source's bibliographic mismatch.
